front: What are the three specialties integrated in multidisciplinary cancer care, and what does each contribute?
back:
Medical Oncology - systemic therapy (chemo, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, hormone therapy)
• Surgical Oncology - local therapy (resection, lymph node sampling, palliative debulking)
• Radiation Oncology - local therapy (curative, palliative, or oligometastatic-directed)

front: Define these cancer treatment-intent terms: curative, palliative, definitive, neoadjuvant, adjuvant, concurrent.
back:
• Curative: intent is to cure
• Palliative: intent is to relieve symptoms
• Definitive: no further treatment is intended
• Neoadjuvant: given as a first step (before another therapy)
• Adjuvant: additional treatment after primary treatment, usually to lower recurrence risk
• Concurrent: given at the same time as another therapy (e.g., concurrent chemoradiation)

front: What is the general 4-step approach to a new cancer patient?
back: Diagnosis (H&P, imaging, biopsy for tissue diagnosis) → Staging (TNM and group stage I-IV, additional imaging/surgery as needed) → Treatment (define curative vs. palliative goal, multidisciplinary consultation) → Follow-up (manage toxicity, periodic exam and restaging). Performance status is also assessed throughout.

front: What is the standard treatment paradigm for glioblastoma (GBM)?
back: Upfront maximal safe resection → concurrent chemoradiation for up to 6 weeks (daily PO temozolomide during RT) → adjuvant chemotherapy for 6-12 months (PO temozolomide days 1-5 every 4 weeks).

front: What is the standard treatment paradigm for stage III non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC)?
back: Concurrent chemoradiation (carboplatin + paclitaxel, or carboplatin + pemetrexed) → adjuvant immunotherapy with durvalumab.

front: What are the "don't forget" pearls to address for essentially every new radiation oncology patient?
back:
• Smoking cessation counseling
• Fertility counseling (before gonadal-affecting treatment)
• Pregnancy test (patients of childbearing potential)
• Genetic counseling (when indicated)

front: What is the fundamental difference between EBRT and brachytherapy?
back: EBRT (external beam radiation therapy): radiation source is outside the body (LINAC delivers photons, electrons, or particle beams). Brachytherapy: radioactive source is placed inside or adjacent to the tumor (intracavitary/interstitial).

front: Contrast LDR and HDR brachytherapy, with an example of each.
back: LDR (low-dose rate): permanently implanted radioactive seeds in one procedure, e.g., prostate seed implants. HDR (high-dose rate): an applicator is placed in the patient and connected to a radioactive source on a wire (contained in an "afterloader") for a few minutes at a time, e.g., intracavitary tandem-based brachytherapy for cervical cancer.

front: How does a LINAC generate the photon beam used for EBRT?
back: Electrons are accelerated toward a tungsten target in the head of the gantry; this interaction produces Bremsstrahlung ("braking") X-rays.

front: What is the key difference in beam delivery between IMRT and VMAT?
back: IMRT: non-uniform beam intensity delivered at fixed gantry angles/fields (segmental "step and shoot" or dynamic continuous MLC motion). VMAT: radiation delivered continuously as the gantry rotates around the patient, with MLCs dynamically modulating intensity throughout the arc.

front: Distinguish SRS from SBRT.
back: Both are highly targeted, ultra-hypofractionated techniques (typically 1-5 fractions with very high dose per fraction). SRS conventionally refers to intracranial (brain) targets (e.g., GammaKnife, CyberKnife). SBRT refers to the same stereotactic approach applied to extracranial body sites.

front: What is the difference between a sequential boost and a simultaneous integrated boost (SIB)?
back: Sequential boost ("cone down"): treat a larger volume to an initial dose, then deliver additional fractions to a smaller boost volume afterward (e.g., 2 Gy/fx x 25 fx to 50 Gy, then 2 Gy/fx x 5 more fx to reach 60 Gy). SIB: different dose-per-fraction levels are delivered to different target volumes simultaneously within the same treatment course (e.g., 2 Gy/fx to 50 Gy and 2.4 Gy/fx to 60 Gy, both over 25 fractions).

front: What imaging modalities can be used for IGRT (image-guided radiotherapy)?
back: MV imaging, kV imaging, CBCT (cone-beam CT), MRI, fluoroscopy, +/- implanted fiducial markers.

front: What are the 4 main types of photon interactions with matter?
back:
1. Coherent (Rayleigh) scattering
2. Photoelectric effect
3. Compton effect
4. Pair production

Probability of each depends on photon energy and the atomic number (Z) of the absorbing material.

front: Describe the photoelectric effect and what its probability depends on.
back: A photon transfers all of its energy to an inner-shell electron, ejecting it; an outer-shell electron then fills the vacancy, releasing a characteristic X-ray and/or Auger electron. Probability is proportional to Z3/E3 - favored at low photon energies and high-Z materials. This is the basis of contrast in diagnostic imaging.

front: What is the Compton effect, and why is it the dominant interaction at therapeutic radiation energies?
back: A photon transfers only part of its energy to an outer-shell electron, ejecting it, while the photon scatters onward with reduced energy. It predominates at ~25 keV to 25 MeV (spans therapeutic range) and its probability depends on electron density of the material, nearly independent of atomic number Z.

front: What is pair production, what is its minimum energy threshold, and is it clinically relevant in typical EBRT?
back: A photon interacts with an atomic nucleus and converts into an electron-positron pair (each 0.511 MeV rest mass), requiring at least 1.022 MeV. Probability is proportional to Z x ln(E). Not a significant clinical concern for beams under 10 MV.

front: What is Bremsstrahlung radiation, and how efficient is its production in a LINAC?
back: "Braking radiation" produced when a charged particle (electron) decelerates and scatters while interacting with a heavy atomic nucleus (e.g., tungsten target), emitting X-rays. The process is highly inefficient (~33%); the average energy of the resulting X-ray beam is about 1/3 to 1/2 the max energy of the incoming electrons.

front: What is the electron beam "5-4-3-2" rule of thumb, for a beam of energy E (MeV)?
back:
• Dmax = E/5
• 90% isodose line ≈ E/3.2-4
• 80% isodose line ≈ E/2.8-3
• Practical range = E/2

Example: a 9 MeV beam has Dmax ≈4.5 cm, 90% IDL ≈2.8 cm, practical range ≈4.5 cm.

front: How do surface dose and depth of Dmax trend with increasing beam energy for photons vs. electrons?
back:
Photons: surface dose is LOWER at higher energies; Dmax is DEEPER at higher energies.
Electrons: surface dose is HIGHER at higher energies; Dmax is also DEEPER at higher energies.

front: What is the Bragg peak, and what is the accepted RBE used for proton therapy dosing?
back: As a proton traverses tissue it loses energy gradually, then deposits most of its energy right at the point it stops (the Bragg peak), with minimal exit dose beyond that depth - higher proton energy gives deeper penetration. Proton RBE = 1.1 (multiply photon-equivalent dose by 1.1); dose may be reported in cobalt Gray equivalent (CGE), though ICRU recommends reporting as DRBE.

front: In craniospinal irradiation (CSI), why is "feathering the junction" performed, and how often?
back: Adjacent field junctions (e.g., between spine fields) create a hot spot at the point of overlap and a cold spot behind it. Shifting the match line superiorly by 0.5-1 cm periodically - typically every 5 fractions (~9 Gy), about once a week - spreads out the cold spot over a larger area to reduce the risk of underdosing.

front: What are the "4 R's of Radiobiology," and why do they justify fractionating treatment?
back: Repair, Repopulation, Redistribution, Reoxygenation. Fractionation exploits differences in how normal tissue and tumor cells repair damage and repopulate, allows radioresistant cells to redistribute into more sensitive cell-cycle phases between fractions, and allows hypoxic tumor cells time to reoxygenate and become more radiosensitive.

front: Contrast direct and indirect action of ionizing radiation.
back:
Direct: charged particles (electrons, protons, alpha particles) directly ionize DNA and produce chemical/biologic damage as they pass through tissue.
Indirect: photons (X-rays, gamma rays) and neutrons are not directly ionizing - they transfer energy to produce fast-moving charged particles or free radicals (e.g., from water) that in turn cause the DNA damage. Most photon-induced DNA damage is indirect, via free radicals.

front: How many single-strand breaks (SSBs) and double-strand breaks (DSBs) occur per 1 Gy of radiation, and which is more clinically important?
back: ~1000 SSBs per Gy: generally easily repaired and not lethal. ~40 DSBs per Gy: the primary driver of radiation-induced cell kill, via lethal chromosome/chromatid aberrations (dicentrics, rings, anaphase bridges) if left unrepaired.

front: Which cell cycle phase is most radiosensitive, and which is most radioresistant? Why?
back: M phase is most radiosensitive. Late S/G2 is most radioresistant, because DNA has already been replicated - if damage occurs, the cell has a homologous template available to accurately repair it (homologous recombination).

front: Compare non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) and homologous recombination (HR) for double-strand break repair.
back:
NHEJ: does not require sequence homology, can occur in G1 (before DNA replication), repairs quickly but is error-prone.
HR: requires sequence homology and an undamaged sister chromatid as template (occurs in late S/G2), is slower but much more accurate.

front: What roles do 53BP1 and BRCA1 play at a DNA double-strand break?
back: Both are recruited downstream of ATM-mediated phosphorylation of H2AX (gamma-H2AX). 53BP1 binds and promotes non-homologous end joining (NHEJ). BRCA1 binds and promotes homologous recombination (HR).

front: Name several genetic syndromes caused by defective DNA repair proteins and their key clinical features.
back:
• Ataxia telangiectasia (ATM mutation): telangiectasias, neurologic symptoms, radiosensitivity, cancer risk (lymphoma/leukemia/breast)
• Xeroderma pigmentosum (nucleotide excision repair): UV photosensitivity, high skin cancer risk
• Lynch syndrome (mismatch repair - MLH1/MSH2/MSH6/PMS2): increased colorectal, endometrial, gastric, ovarian cancer risk
• SCID / LIG4 deficiency (NHEJ defects): immunodeficiency and radiosensitivity
• Fanconi anemia (crosslink repair): pancytopenia, growth delay, leukemia risk

front: Define OER and LET, and describe how they relate to each other as radiation becomes more densely ionizing.
back:
OER (oxygen enhancement ratio) = dose needed under hypoxic conditions divided by dose needed under aerobic conditions to achieve the same biologic effect (oxygen "fixes" free-radical DNA damage). LET (linear energy transfer) = energy deposited per unit track length (keV/µm).
As LET increases (more densely ionizing radiation, e.g., alpha particles > neutrons > x-rays), OER decreases: OER is ~2.5-3 for x-/gamma-rays and protons, ~1.6 for neutrons, and ~1 (none) for alpha particles.

front: What is the alpha/beta ratio, and how does it differ between early- and late-responding tissue?
back: The alpha/beta ratio is the dose at which the linear (single-hit, alpha) and quadratic (double-hit, beta) components of cell killing are equal. Early-responding tissues (most tumors, skin, GI mucosa, bone marrow) have a HIGH alpha/beta (~10). Late-responding tissues (prostate, breast, spinal cord, lung, kidney, liver, bladder) have a LOW alpha/beta (~3; spinal cord ~2) and are more sensitive to dose per fraction.

front: Give the formulas for Biologically Effective Dose (BED) and EQD2, and state what drives acute vs. late radiation toxicity.
back:
BED = n x d x [1 + d/(alpha/beta)] (n = number of fractions, d = dose per fraction)
EQD2 = D x [(d + alpha/beta)/(2 + alpha/beta)] (D = total dose)
Acute toxicity is characterized by inflammation and is a function of total dose. Late toxicity is characterized by fibrosis/sclerosis and is a function of dose per fraction (best assessed with BED).

front: How does toxicity risk differ between "series" and "parallel" organs at risk?
back:
Series organs (e.g., spinal cord, brainstem, optic nerves, bowel): toxicity depends on maximum/point dose - "if you poke a hole in it, the whole thing breaks."
Parallel organs (e.g., lung, liver, kidney, parotid gland): toxicity depends on volumetric or mean dose - "if you damage enough of it, it breaks."

front: Per QUANTEC, what is the conventional-fractionation spinal cord max dose constraint, and how does myelopathy risk rise above it?
back: Max dose <50 Gy (2 Gy/fx) → <0.3% risk of myelopathy. Risk rises steeply beyond that: 50 Gy ≈0.2%, 60 Gy ≈6%, 69 Gy ≈50%.

front: What are the QUANTEC conventional-fractionation max dose constraints for brain, brainstem, and optic nerves/chiasm?
back: Brain: max <60 Gy (<3% symptomatic necrosis). Brainstem: max <54 Gy (<5% neuropathy or necrosis). Optic nerves/chiasm: max <55 Gy (<3% optic neuropathy).

front: What is the classic QUANTEC lung dose constraint, and what toxicity does it predict?
back: V20 ≤30% (volume of lung receiving ≥20 Gy) → predicts <20% risk of symptomatic pneumonitis.

front: Per HYTEC, what are the approximate spinal cord Dmax constraints for SRS/SBRT to keep myelopathy risk at 1-5%?
back: 1 fraction: 12.4 Gy • 2 fractions: 17 Gy • 3 fractions: 20.3 Gy • 4 fractions: 23 Gy • 5 fractions: 25.3 Gy (Sahgal et al., 2013).

front: Define GTV, CTV, ITV, and PTV.
back:
GTV = gross tumor volume (visible/palpable tumor)
CTV = clinical target volume (GTV + margin for suspected microscopic disease)
ITV = internal target volume (CTV + margin for internal organ motion)
PTV = planning target volume (adds margin for daily setup uncertainty)

front: Define OAR and PRV.
back: OAR = organ at risk (normal structure that could be damaged by radiation). PRV = planning risk volume (margin added around an OAR to account for setup/motion uncertainty, analogous to how PTV relates to CTV).

front: What does DIBH stand for, and why is it used?
back: Deep inspiratory breath hold - a motion-management technique (commonly used for left-sided breast radiation) in which the patient holds a deep breath during treatment, expanding lung volume and pulling the heart away from the treatment field to reduce cardiac dose.

front: Compare FBCT (fan-beam/helical CT) and CBCT (cone-beam CT), and what each is used for.
back:
FBCT: diagnostic-quality imaging, higher radiation dose, better soft-tissue resolution, takes longer - used for simulation/diagnostic imaging.
CBCT: lower radiation dose, faster, can focus on smaller areas - used for daily IGRT setup verification.

front: What do the oncologic outcome acronyms OS, PFS, DFS, EFS, and DMFS stand for?
back:
OS = overall survival
PFS = progression-free survival
DFS = disease-free survival
EFS = event-free survival
DMFS = distant metastasis-free survival

front: What is the difference between Dose (Gy) and MU (monitor units)?
back: Dose (measured in Gray, Gy) is what is prescribed and represents the biologic dose delivered to the patient. MU (monitor unit) is the unit the LINAC machine actually measures and delivers to produce that prescribed dose.
